chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: What an AI-Local System is
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] What an AI-Local System is
For most small businesses, AI currently means opening a chat tool, asking a
question, generating some copy, and returning to business as usual. That is
useful. It is not the transformation.

The larger opportunity begins when AI is connected to the actual operating
environment of the business: its website, code, customer enquiries, content,
analytics, documents, workflows, business rules and approval processes. That is an
AI-Local System.

It changes the question from "what can AI generate for me?" to "what parts of my
business can now become faster, smarter and continuously improvable?"

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: The website becomes a layer, not the product
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] The website becomes a layer, not the product
Traditionally a website is a finished object: build it, launch it, update it
occasionally, redesign it in a few years.

In an AI-Local System the website becomes the visible layer of a larger digital
operating system. Behind it sit an AI-assisted development environment, version
history, business knowledge, analytics, customer information, automation and
controlled approval. The website stops being something the business owns and
becomes something it can continuously operate and improve.

A general AI chat may know how to write a landing page. It cannot see the existing
one, understand the company's structure, modify the right files, build a safe
preview, compare it against the original and put it up for approval.

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: Continuous improvement instead of projects
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] Continuous improvement instead of projects
Traditional digital work moves in large jumps: hire someone, request changes, the
project ends, months pass, another project begins.

Connected infrastructure makes smaller continuous improvements possible instead. A
headline gets tested. A service page gets created. Customer questions become FAQs.
A successful campaign becomes a reusable template. Weak pages get identified.
Content gets refreshed. Each improvement becomes part of the existing system
rather than another isolated project, and over time they compound.

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: The gap between using AI and integrating it
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] The gap between using AI and integrating it
McKinsey's 2025 research frames the opportunity:

- 88 percent of surveyed organizations use AI in at least one business function.
- 7 percent have fully scaled it across the organization.
- 92 percent planned to increase AI investment over the following three years.
- Around 1 percent of executives described their organization as mature in AI
  deployment.

The technology arrived faster than most organizations learned how to operationalize
it. The organizations generating the most value are the ones redesigning workflows,
not the ones adding an AI tool on top of an existing process.

Large companies are not simply buying AI subscriptions. They are investing in
integrating AI into workflows. That gap is the whole opportunity.

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: Why this matters more for a small business
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] Why this matters more for a small business
A large corporation can staff separate teams for development, marketing, analytics,
customer support, automation, data and infrastructure. A small company cannot, and
that has always been a technological disadvantage.

AI compresses the gap, not by replacing those specialists, but because a smaller
number of capable people can now operate across a much larger surface area. One
person with the right system can coordinate work that previously took several
contractors, tools and agencies.

The old stack is a website plus email plus social plus assorted software, with
manual work in between: each piece useful, none aware of the others. The emerging
model connects them, and the connection is where the value is.

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: Human control stays in the loop
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] Human control stays in the loop
AI-Local does not mean letting AI freely change a business. The strongest
architecture keeps a person in the loop, buying speed without giving up control.
For a small business that combination is the point: fast enough to be worth
having, controlled enough to be safe to run.

A company does not need the most advanced stage immediately. It needs an
architecture capable of reaching it.

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: Why the advantage is not "using AI"
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] Why the advantage is not "using AI"
Soon, saying a company uses AI will mean almost nothing, because most will. The
questions that separate businesses are different:

- How deeply is AI connected to the business?
- What information can it actually reach?
- What actions can it safely perform?
- What workflows does it accelerate?
- What does the company learn from the resulting data?
- How fast can an idea become execution?

The next advantage is unlikely to come from access to the best model. Thousands of
businesses can reach the same models. The advantage comes from what surrounds it:
business data, systems, workflows, tools, rules and human approval. That
combination is much harder to copy.

chunks.title: AI-Local Systems for Small Business
chunks.heading: Compounding returns
chunks.content:
[AI-Local Systems for Small Business] Compounding returns
A better website generates enquiries. The assistant understands them. Those
conversations reveal the questions. The questions become content. The content
brings traffic. The traffic creates data. Each cycle makes the system more useful.

The opportunity is not to automate a few tasks. It is to build a business that can
learn, execute and improve faster than it could before. The website can be the
starting point without being the ending point: the front door to an intelligent
system connecting marketing, customers, operations, data and continuous
improvement. Not another AI tool, but an intelligent layer around the business.

chunks.title: FAQ
chunks.heading: How much analyst time does the deal copilot save?
chunks.content:
[FAQ] How much analyst time does the deal copilot save?
Most teams recover 20–50 hours per deal by reducing document hunting, memo drafting,
and diligence synthesis.

Where the time comes back:

- Questions about deal documents answered in seconds, with sources, instead of hours of searching.
- IC memo sections (risks, business overview, market) drafted from diligence materials, so senior people review instead of write.
- Inconsistencies between commercial, financial, and legal diligence flagged before the IC meeting.

chunks.title: FAQ
chunks.heading: Can you build X?
chunks.content:
[FAQ] Can you build X?
Probably, if it fits the philosophy of building production-grade systems around real workflows and data.

If you have a specific idea, briefly describe:

- The workflow you want to improve.
- The tools and data you already use.
- Any hard constraints (compliance, latency, integrations).

The best next step is a short scope call to see if CAI is the right fit.

chunks.title: FAQ
chunks.heading: How do we get started?
chunks.content:
[FAQ] How do we get started?
The path is simple:

1. Share a short description of your project and constraints.
2. Do a scope call to map the work and risks.
3. Review a written plan and quote.

If you are ready now, you can send your details in this three-line format:

Name: <your name>
Email: <your email>
Project: <one-line description>

CAI will follow up by email to schedule a call.

chunks.title: FAQ
chunks.heading: What does it cost?
chunks.content:
[FAQ] What does it cost?
CAI does not publish a fixed price list. What a project costs is quoted after a
scope call, and CAI charges per project rather than per hour.

What the market charges in 2026, read across six published pricing guides:

- Simple AI chatbot: $10,000 to $30,000.
- Custom RAG and business chatbot: $30,000 to $70,000.
- Advanced AI system with integrations and support: $60,000 to $150,000+.

Those are market ranges, useful for sanity-checking any proposal. They are not a
CAI price list, and CAI does not quote against them without knowing the scope.

What decides the band is how much of the business the system has to understand and
safely act on, not which AI model is behind it. Answering questions sits low.
Answering from your own documents, prices and policies sits in the middle. Taking
actions and connecting to live systems sits at the top.

Budget for the running cost as well: maintenance runs 15 to 25 percent of the
build per year across this market.

How CAI structures payment on a project:

- A 50% deposit to begin work.
- The remainder on delivery milestones.

chunks.title: FAQ
chunks.heading: Do you work with small teams or only large companies?
chunks.content:
[FAQ] Do you work with small teams or only large companies?
Both. What matters is:

- The importance of the workflow or decision you are improving.
- Whether there is a clear owner on your side.
- Whether we can draw a straight line from the system to business value.

chunks.title: FAQ
chunks.heading: What models and tools do you use?
chunks.content:
[FAQ] What models and tools do you use?
CAI is model- and vendor-agnostic.

The focus is on:

- Choosing models that fit the problem and constraints.
- Designing the surrounding system so it is observable, debuggable, and changeable.
- Avoiding unnecessary complexity.

The exact tools and models are chosen per engagement and can evolve over time.

chunks.title: How CAI Engagements Run
chunks.heading: 1. Scope
chunks.content:
[How CAI Engagements Run] 1. Scope
- A short scope call to understand:
  - The workflow or decision you want to improve.
  - The systems and data already in place.
  - Constraints around latency, security, and ownership.
- The goal is to define a narrow, high-leverage slice of work.

chunks.title: How CAI Engagements Run
chunks.heading: 2. Plan
chunks.content:
[How CAI Engagements Run] 2. Plan
After the call, CAI provides:

- A concise description of the proposed system.
- The boundaries: what it will and will not do.
- A rough timeline and implementation approach.
- A quote and payment structure.

CAI's price is quoted per engagement after this call, never taken off a list.
Market ranges can indicate the likely band beforehand; the quote itself follows
the scope.
Projects typically start with a 50% deposit to begin work.

chunks.title: How CAI Engagements Run
chunks.heading: 3. Build
chunks.content:
[How CAI Engagements Run] 3. Build
CAI then:

- Designs the architecture and data flows.
- Implements the system, wiring into existing tools where possible.
- Adds instrumentation and basic operational tooling so the team can trust it.

The emphasis is on shipping something small but real, not a prototype that never leaves a sandbox.

chunks.title: How CAI Engagements Run
chunks.heading: 4. Deploy and Iterate
chunks.content:
[How CAI Engagements Run] 4. Deploy and Iterate
Once the system is in real use:

- CAI monitors behavior with you.
- Tightens failure modes and guardrails.
- Iterates based on actual usage, not assumptions.

Handover is structured so your team can own and extend the system over time.

chunks.title: Abstracted Proof Projects
chunks.heading: Venue Audio Operations Assistant
chunks.content:
[Abstracted Proof Projects] Venue Audio Operations Assistant
Context:

- A multi-room live events venue needed to run complex audio setups reliably without requiring a senior engineer in every room.
- Information about room layouts, equipment, presets, and failure playbooks lived in scattered documents and institutional memory.

What CAI built:

- A workflow assistant that operators could query in natural language from a tablet or laptop.
- A retrieval layer over venue documentation: room diagrams, patch lists, routing plans, and troubleshooting guides.
- Logic that translated operator questions ("We plugged this into that and there's no sound, what now?") into precise, step-by-step actions.

Outcomes:

- Faster setup and recovery from issues.
- Reduced reliance on a few experts.
- A documented, inspectable system instead of oral tradition.

chunks.title: Abstracted Proof Projects
chunks.heading: M&A Deal Intelligence Hub
chunks.content:
[Abstracted Proof Projects] M&A Deal Intelligence Hub
Context:

- An acquirer with many deals-in-flight needed one place to reason about targets, risks, and rationale.
- Information lived in decks, memos, data rooms, and email threads.

What CAI built:

- A hub that ingested structured deal trackers and unstructured materials (memos, attachments, notes).
- A retrieval system that let the team ask questions like:
  - "Show me everything we know about this target's go-to-market risks."
  - "Summarize the key drivers of this deal next to the open questions."
- Views tuned for decision-making, not for generic chat.

Outcomes:

- Faster preparation for investment committees.
- Less time hunting for "that one slide" or memo.
- A shared mental model of each deal that updated as new information arrived.

chunks.title: Abstracted Proof Projects
chunks.heading: Engineering Knowledge RAG Stack
chunks.content:
[Abstracted Proof Projects] Engineering Knowledge RAG Stack
Context:

- An engineering team had critical documentation spread across repos, wikis, and issue trackers.
- New engineers struggled to answer "how do we do X here?" without pinging senior people.

What CAI built:

- A RAG stack that ingested code-adjacent docs, runbooks, and architecture notes.
- A query layer optimized for questions like:
  - "How do we deploy service Y?"
  - "What are the failure modes of this subsystem and how do we detect them?"
- Guardrails so answers surfaced only what was actually written, without inventing details.

Outcomes:

- Faster onboarding and fewer interruptions to senior engineers.
- Clearer documentation gaps, since unanswered queries highlighted missing materials.

chunks.title: CAI Service Lines
chunks.heading: 1. Workflow & Agent Systems
chunks.content:
[CAI Service Lines] 1. Workflow & Agent Systems
Design and build AI-assisted workflows and agents that own a business process from end to end.

Examples of outcomes:

- Intake and triage for complex requests, with AI translating free-form input into structured actions.
- Agents that monitor tools (tickets, emails, docs) and propose or execute the next step.
- Orchestration layers that coordinate multiple tools, APIs, and models to complete a workflow.

Key characteristics:

- Built around real constraints: latency, access control, failure modes.
- Instrumented for observability so teams can trust and debug behavior.
- Designed so the team can own it after handoff.

chunks.title: CAI Service Lines
chunks.heading: 2. RAG & Knowledge Systems
chunks.content:
[CAI Service Lines] 2. RAG & Knowledge Systems
Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that let teams ask natural language questions over their own knowledge.

Typical sources:

- Internal docs and wikis.
- Deal rooms, research memos, and spreadsheets.
- Engineering documentation and runbooks.

Focus areas:

- Clean ingestion and normalization of heterogeneous sources.
- Honest retrieval (no silent hallucinations about what the corpus does not contain).
- Interfaces that match how the team actually asks questions.

chunks.title: CAI Service Lines
chunks.heading: 3. Applied ML & Data Platforms
chunks.content:
[CAI Service Lines] 3. Applied ML & Data Platforms
Design and implement applied ML systems and data pipelines where correctness and reliability matter.

Examples:

- Ranking, scoring, or prioritization models that feed human workflows.
- Data processing and feature pipelines that prepare inputs for downstream models.
- Batch and streaming jobs with monitoring and alerting.

The emphasis is on systems that ship and stay healthy in production over time.

chunks.title: CAI Service Lines
chunks.heading: 4. Advisory, Architecture, and Reviews
chunks.content:
[CAI Service Lines] 4. Advisory, Architecture, and Reviews
Short, focused advisory work to help teams make better decisions about AI systems.

Examples:

- Architecture reviews for existing or planned AI systems.
- Vendor and tool selection guidance anchored in real constraints.
- Risk and reliability reviews for AI-heavy flows.

This work often leads into a build engagement when there is a clear path to value.

chunks.title: Custom AI Models (CAI) — Overview
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Models (CAI) — Overview]
# Custom AI Models (CAI) — Overview

Custom AI Models (CAI) is the solo consultancy of Yeriko Vargas, a senior AI/ML systems engineer.
CAI focuses on designing and shipping production-grade AI systems that plug into a client's existing tools and data.
The work is hands-on: architecture, implementation, and deployment, not just slideware.

CAI is best for teams who:

- Have high-value workflows that are currently manual or brittle.
- Have fragmented data across tools, docs, and systems.
- Care about reliability, latency, and observability — not just demos.
- Want a partner who can reason about both product and infrastructure.

The engagement style is pragmatic and technical:

- Map the workflow and constraints in detail.
- Design the smallest useful system that can own the workflow end-to-end.
- Ship to production quickly, then iterate.

All examples and proof are anonymized. CAI never names confidential clients or venues.
CAI's own price is quoted per engagement and finalized after a short scope call,
with a 50% deposit to start work. Published 2026 market ranges are a sanity check
on any proposal, not a CAI price list.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026]
# Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026

Research published by CAI in the article "What Custom AI Actually Costs in 2026".
Six development firms published 2026 pricing guides; read together and converted to
one currency, they resolve into three bands. These are market ranges, not a CAI
price list. CAI quotes each engagement after a scope call.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: The three market bands
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] The three market bands
Indicative 2026 build cost, in US dollars, across the published guides:

- Band 1, simple AI chatbot: $10,000 to $30,000. Answers questions in natural
  language, with one or two systems behind it.
- Band 2, custom RAG and business chatbot: $30,000 to $70,000. Answers from the
  company's own documents, prices, policies and history.
- Band 3, advanced AI system with integrations and support: $60,000 to $150,000+.
  Takes actions, connects to live systems, and is maintained and optimised over time.

Below band 1 sits the plain FAQ widget at roughly $3,800 to $7,600, which is on a
different ladder entirely. Above band 3, full enterprise deployments are published
at $76,000 to $317,000 and up.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: What moves a build between bands
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] What moves a build between bands
The band is decided by how much of the business the system has to understand and
safely act on. It is not decided by which AI model is behind it.

Three questions place a build:

- How much of your own information does it need to know? None, and it is band 1.
  Your documents, prices and policies, and it is band 2.
- Does it need to do things, or only say things? Actions, integrations and live
  systems are what move a project into band 3.
- Who keeps it correct next year? Every guide charges for that separately.

Most small businesses do not need band 3, and are quoted for it anyway.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Why a chatbot and an AI system are different products
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Why a chatbot and an AI system are different products
A chatbot is cheap. A widget answering from a list of pre-written responses is a
small piece of software. An AI system knows the company: it retrieves documents,
prices and policies accurately, follows the business rules and tone, connects to
the tools already in use, and stays correct as the business changes underneath it.

Same conversation box on the screen. Different thing behind it, by an order of
magnitude in engineering and in price. A quote should make clear which of the two
it is for.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Why RAG changes the price
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Why RAG changes the price
RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is the step that lets a system answer from a
company's own information instead of from whatever the model absorbed in training.
Answering from a company's own information is the single biggest jump on the
ladder, and the reason is not the model. The work being paid for is selecting and
structuring the documents the system may see, building and tuning the retrieval so
it returns the right passage rather than a plausible one, an evaluation harness
that proves it keeps doing so, guardrails for what must never be said or invented,
and the authentication, logging and update paths that let it be changed safely.

One firm prices that layer alone at $25,400 to $69,900 for production. The model
subscription inside it costs a few dollars a month.

This is the step that makes a custom system expensive, and it is expensive for
reasons that have nothing to do with the model subscription. Retrieval is where a
build stops being a widget and starts being infrastructure.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Where the money actually goes
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Where the money actually goes
Six blocks of work, and only one of them is the AI model:

- Business data: which documents, databases and policies the system may see.
- Retrieval: search that pulls the right context for every question.
- The model: the cheapest line on the invoice.
- Interface: the chat surface, internal tools and APIs people actually touch.
- Testing: evaluation sets and iteration, so accuracy is a number, not a feeling.
- Monitoring: logs, guardrails and adjustment as rules and teams keep changing.

Two systems can run the same model and cost wildly different amounts. The
difference is the shape and depth of the other five blocks.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Why "just use ChatGPT or Claude" is not enough
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Why "just use ChatGPT or Claude" is not enough
General models are trained on the public internet. They do not know a specific
business: not its pricing rules, not its contract terms, not its edge cases, not
the tone its team uses when something has gone wrong. Used raw they generalise,
they guess, and under pressure they invent. That is survivable in an internal
brainstorm. It is not survivable in a system that talks to customers or touches
money.

Four things change that, and all four are engineering rather than licensing:
retrieval makes the model read approved content before it answers, guardrails set
what it may say and do, testing turns "it seems good" into a number, and
monitoring allows it to be tightened when the real world pushes back.

Every serious 2026 guide is organised around data, retrieval, testing and
integration, not around which model was chosen. The model is necessary. It is
nowhere near sufficient.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: What a quoted range does not include
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] What a quoted range does not include
A published range usually prices one layer, not the whole stack. A retrieval price
does not buy the website, the environment where it can be changed under
supervision with previews and rollback, the integrations, or anyone maintaining it
next year. Those are separate line items in every guide. The only honest way to
read a price is to ask what fraction of the stack it covers.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Add-ons priced on top
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Add-ons priced on top
Published separately, once a client asks for anything beyond conversation:

- Agentic workflows, meaning tools and multi-step execution: $20,000 to $60,000.
- Each major live-system integration: $10,000 to $30,000.
- Multimodal input: $15,000 to $40,000.
- Multi-language support: $8,000 to $25,000.
- Annual maintenance: 15 to 25 percent of the build, every year.

The first line is the one to read twice. The ability for the system to actually do
things, the step from band 2 to band 3, is priced on its own at up to $60,000.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Running cost after launch
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Running cost after launch
Build price is not the whole number. Ongoing operation is published at $1,000 to
$15,000 a month, and annual maintenance at 15 to 25 percent of the build. On a
$75,000 system that is $11,250 to $18,750 a year before anyone writes a new line
of code.

A system that is genuinely maintained carries a running cost everywhere in this
market. Any quote without one is either excluding it or hiding it.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: How serious firms structure the money
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] How serious firms structure the money
- A year-one project fee covering design, build, rollout and an agreed period of
  support, usually six to twelve months. This is the band 1, 2 or 3 number.
- Year-one support and tooling bundled into that fee.
- Optional years after that, as a separately scoped annual package rather than a
  quiet assumption.
- A reconnection fee if support stops and the client returns later, because the
  system, its data and its guardrails have to be brought back to a safe state.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: Where these numbers come from
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] Where these numbers come from
Nine published ranges from six firms: Kellton, Cleveroad, Sharp Code, Fulminous,
Emvigo and Seven Solvers. Sterling figures were converted at one pound to $1.27.
Every figure is linked to its source page in the published article, so any of them
can be checked. Prices move; the article notes that if a guide has been revised
since, its page will say so.

The spread between the guides is not disagreement. It is six firms pricing
different products and calling them all a chatbot.

chunks.title: Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026
chunks.heading: The one line worth keeping
chunks.content:
[Custom AI Market Pricing in 2026] The one line worth keeping
You are not paying for access to an AI model. You are paying to turn a general
model into a reliable system built around your business. The engineering is the
product.
